newsitem.title: UK: Economic strategist sees market turmoil by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Economic strategist sees market turmoil by 2000.

text.p: William Houston, British author of a series of books warning business about the ominously cyclical behaviour of history, climate and markets, is predicting a global collapse of bond and stock markets between now and the start of the 21st century.

Houston, a 68-year-old former weapons officer in the British Navy, turned lecturer and company doctor, publishes his predictions and their consequences in his latest book "Through the Whirlwind -Strategies for Survival."

"It would only take one (G7 country) default for government bond markets round the world to dry up ... no investor would trust the bond market, also making it extremely difficult for the stock markets to hold up," he said.

"This is the history of cycles -- we're going to see problems like earthquakes and disease piling up in the next century. Investors should also look at the 1929 (the Wall Street crash) parallels," he added.

Houston is part of an honourable, if somewhat eccentric, tradition of economic forecasting going back at least to the mid-19th century, tracing a raft of metereological, disease, economic and historical cycles spanning scores of decades or even one that recurs every 500 years.

A board member of the Foundation for the Study of Cycles -- putting him in the upper echelons of cycle gurus, he uses historical parallels to anticipate contemporary crises. In one case he compared Henry VIII's break with Rome in the 1500s with the likely consequences in the 1990s of Britain rejecting full European union.
According to Houston, cycle adherents agree the most influential cycle in recent times is the Kondratieff 45-60 year "long wave," named after its originator, a Russian economist of the 1920s.

Studying historic interest rates, commodity and finished goods prices in Britain, the United States and France, the Russian concluded economies at various times moved in distinct phases -- the upwave, a period of expansion out of recession; an in-between phase called the plateau stage; and the downwave marking the return to recession. Kondratieff predicted the deep depression in the 1930s using his observations. The state later sent him to Siberia.
Today, Houston says, "a highly singular confluence of important cycles (including the Kondratieff long wave) are reaching their low point."
Other possible contributors to turmoil include a cycle that produces major social upsets every 500 years and one that triggers climatic and historical changes during a 179-year drought cycle.

Houston sees contemporary financial markets riding an economic downwave that started in 1990, the symptoms of which include recession, rising real interest rates, a collapse of credit and mounting national debts.
The last of these -- crippling debts -- may prove the final straw for markets, says Houston.

"Corporate and public institutions' debts are reckoned currently to be running at $20 trillion compared with world GDP of some $25 trillion, which puts leverage at about 80 percent. But this doesn't take account of about $50 trillion in off-balance sheet or derivative debts," Houston said.

The debt mountain will weigh ever more heavily on bond markets. Houston believes the one-time failure of an indebted Western country like Italy or Sweden to service its loans, or even a natural disaster -- a huge earthquake centred in Tokyo for example -- could trigger a fatal collapse in capital markets.

"A Tokyo quake, part of a 70-year cycle in rising seismic activity, would affect some 5 percent of the world's GDP. There would be a huge sucking noise of securities being repatriated to pay for what could amount to $5 trillion in damages," he said.
Also any rise in the price of wheat -- prompted in the next few years by the return of cool, dry climates -- would fan the flames of inflation and mete out further damage to bonds.
"The best investments would be food processing, mining, precious metals or energy stocks and probably gold," he said.
While stocks could remain a good alternative in the short-term, Houston is convinced equity markets would falter in the face of crumbling bond markets.

The implications for governments if stock and bond markets collapse, as Houston forsees it, may include a gradual reduction in their influence over individuals as the state runs out of funds to keep afloat centralized services such as education, welfare and healthcare.
